metrics.name: GPU memory usage
metrics.caveat: The paper emphasizes that accuracy alone does not capture deployment suitability and considers GPU memory usage alongside accuracy and inference speed.

controls.name: PatchCore without importance re-weighting (neighbour number 1)

controls.rules_out: That the reported noise-resilience improvement from importance re-weighting is present without re-weighting.

controls.name: Vanilla few-shot training without augmentation
controls.detail: Compared with rotation-augmented training at the same shot counts.
controls.rules_out: That rotation-augmentation results merely reflect the few-shot training condition rather than augmentation.

controls.name: Alternative few-shot augmentations
controls.detail: Flip, scale, translate, ColorJitter, and perspective augmentation are compared with rotation at the same shot counts.
controls.rules_out: That any tested augmentation produces the same effect as rotation.

confounds.name: Differences in anomaly type, rather than general method quality, explain performance differences
confounds.detail: The paper notes that methods suited to structural anomalies may perform differently on logical anomalies, which could account for apparent performance differences across datasets.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On MVTec LOCO-AD, report image AUROC and pixel sPRO separately for logical and structural anomalies, as well as their means.

datasets.name: MVTec AD 2
datasets.eval_protocol: Eight scenarios; training and validation contain only defect-free images, and training uses regular lighting. The public test set includes a small labeled sample across lighting conditions. The private test set uses training lighting; the private mixed test set randomly combines seen and unseen lighting conditions. Reported localization uses AU-PRO integrated to FPR 0.05. For thresholded F1, the segmentation threshold is the mean per-pixel anomaly value on defect-free validation images plus 3 standard deviations. Images are resized to 256×256 unless otherwise stated; RD/RD++ use the next smaller side length divisible by 32. Higher-resolution experiments are also reported.

datasets.name: MVTec AD
datasets.eval_protocol: Compared in the paper’s established-dataset table using segmentation AU-PRO integrated to FPR 0.30. RD and RD++ results are taken from their cited original papers.

datasets.name: VisA
datasets.eval_protocol: Compared in the paper’s established-dataset table using segmentation AU-PRO integrated to FPR 0.30. For RD, RD++, and MSFlow, VisA results are derived using the same parameters as for MVTec AD.

baselines.fair_comparison: Official implementation and default settings; input images are 256×256 unless otherwise stated. Uses the default ensemble (WideResNet-101, ResNeXT-101, DenseNet-201), 0.01% approximate greedy coreset sampling, and 384-dimensional aggregated embeddings; center cropping is disabled for border defects.

baselines.name: Reverse Distillation Revisited (RD++)
baselines.fair_comparison: Official implementation and MVTec AD settings, without scenario-specific hyperparameter tuning. Uses the same next-smaller-multiple-of-32 resizing procedure as RD. MVTec AD results are taken from the original paper; VisA uses the same parameters as MVTec AD.

baselines.name: MSFlow
baselines.fair_comparison: Official implementation; uses 256×256 training and inference images for comparison with the other methods rather than the 512×512 setting. VisA results use the same parameters as MVTec AD.

baselines.fair_comparison: Official implementation with a WideResNet50 feature extractor; trained for 160 epochs, following the cited setting, without scenario-specific training-duration tuning.

metrics.name: AU-PRO (AU-PRO0.05 and AU-PRO0.30)
metrics.caveat: AU-ROC/TPR can be dominated by large defects and overstate localization when smaller defects are missed; PRO weights anomalous regions equally. The paper uses the stricter FPR integration limit of 0.05 for MVTec AD 2 because 0.30 can permit excessively large segmented regions, and reports 0.30 for comparison on established datasets.

metrics.name: Pixel-level F1
metrics.caveat: A threshold-dependent score need not track threshold-independent AU-PRO; the paper reports both and derives the threshold from defect-free validation data as the mean per-pixel anomaly value plus 3 standard deviations.

metrics.name: Image-level F1
metrics.caveat: Threshold-dependent and may not track threshold-independent localization performance; the image decision uses the same segmentation threshold, with the maximum pixel anomaly value as the image score.

metrics.name: Inference runtime
metrics.caveat: Runtime alone does not capture memory constraints; the paper reports peak memory alongside it. Measured on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti as the mean of 1,000 forward passes after a warm-up of the same duration, batch size 1, float32; timing includes transfer to GPU and return of the anomaly image to CPU.

metrics.name: Peak GPU memory usage
metrics.caveat: Memory alone does not capture runtime constraints; the paper reports inference runtime alongside it. Measured on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti using PyTorch reserved peak memory; PatchCore timing uses the combined public and private test data and averages inference over approximately 200 samples after warm-up.

confounds.name: Small or low-contrast defects disappear when images are resized to the standard input resolution
confounds.detail: The paper considers whether the poor results at 256×256 reflect information lost during preprocessing rather than the difficulty of the anomaly-detection methods.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It evaluates increased input sizes, up to half the original image height and width, and measures AU-PRO, runtime, and memory; larger inputs substantially improve localization for some methods, while increasing computational cost.

confounds.name: Test-set overfitting or excessive tuning could inflate benchmark results
confounds.detail: If hyperparameters were selected using test ground truth, scores could reflect tuning to known defects rather than unsupervised generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The private test-set ground truth is held by the evaluation server. The stated protocol derives hyperparameters and thresholds from defect-free validation images, with the public test set available only for optional initial estimation.

controls.name: Full-image input with shared masked-region information
controls.detail: The ablation keeps the masking ratio at 0.4 and varies the masking unit q from 1 to 112 pixels; at q=16, the information is the same as MMR's input, but masked-region features are shared with visible regions.
controls.rules_out: A performance gain explained by the masking ratio alone or by information leakage from visible regions; the paper reports lower performance than MMR for the shared-information q=16 condition.

controls.name: Masking-ratio ablation
controls.detail: Tests masking ratios from 0 to 0.9.
controls.rules_out: That the reported result is independent of masking, and shows how performance changes when the masked-recovery condition is removed or made more extreme.

controls.name: Feature-scale ablation
controls.detail: Compares using individual encoder layers and combinations of layers instead of all three scales.
controls.rules_out: That the result depends on using all feature scales equally; the reported comparisons measure the contribution of each scale and their combinations.

controls.name: ViT trained from scratch
controls.detail: Replaces the ImageNet masked-autoencoder-pretrained ViT with one trained from scratch.
controls.rules_out: That the reported performance does not depend on the ViT pre-training condition.

controls.name: Alternative frozen hierarchical encoders
controls.detail: Compares random-initialized ResNet-18, pre-trained ResNet-18, and WideResNet50 as the frozen encoder.
controls.rules_out: That the result is specific to only one frozen encoder choice.

confounds.name: Visible-region information leakage could make masked recovery appear effective
confounds.detail: If features from visible regions are shared with masked regions, the model could recover masked content from leaked local information rather than infer it from broader spatial relationships.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The input-form ablation compares shared-information masking to MMR's fully hidden masked patches; the paper reports lower performance for the shared-information q=16 condition.

confounds.name: The first MMR part could take an identical shortcut and simply reproduce the frozen encoder's output
confounds.detail: If its output were identical to the frozen encoder's output, detection performance would not establish that the trained reconstruction part contributes useful anomaly information.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper compares the anomaly visualizations and reports that MMR detects tiny defects, which it takes as evidence that the first part avoids the identical shortcut.

baselines.fair_comparison: The authors report evaluating AdaCLIP under AnomalyCLIP's experimental setting; AnomalyCLIP itself was not directly compared because its implementation was unavailable.

controls.name: No static or dynamic prompts (V1)
controls.detail: Ablation with both static and dynamic prompts removed.
controls.rules_out: Provides the no-prompt reference for testing whether adding prompts improves performance.

controls.name: Static prompts only (V2)
controls.detail: Ablation with static prompts enabled and dynamic prompts removed.
controls.rules_out: Compared with V1, tests whether static prompts contribute; compared with V4, tests whether static prompts alone account for the hybrid-prompt result.

controls.name: Dynamic prompts only (V3)
controls.detail: Ablation with dynamic prompts enabled and static prompts removed.
controls.rules_out: Compared with V1, tests whether dynamic prompts contribute; compared with V4, tests whether dynamic prompts alone account for the hybrid-prompt result.

controls.name: HSF removed
controls.detail: Image-level anomaly detection without HSF, using the maximum anomaly-map value.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the image-level result depends on HSF rather than the maximum-based alternative.

confounds.name: Prompt gains may be offset by overfitting from added learnable parameters
confounds.detail: The paper notes that increasing prompting depth or length adds learnable parameters and may overfit the auxiliary training data, which could explain why larger prompt configurations do not improve generalization.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Evaluate performance across prompting depths J and lengths M; the paper reports that performance does not improve continuously with larger settings and selects J=4, M=5 for high performance across both domains.

confounds.name: Maximum anomaly-map values may be sensitive to noisy predictions
confounds.detail: The paper notes that conventional image-level scoring by taking the maximum anomaly-map value can be sensitive to noisy predictions, potentially affecting image-level comparisons.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare image-level performance with HSF enabled against the HSF-removed, maximum-based condition in the ablation study.

datasets.name: Real-IAD Variety
datasets.eval_protocol: Train/test split: 3,991 normal samples (19,955 images) for training; 35,799 samples for testing (3,990 normal and 31,809 anomalous; 178,995 images). The test set is described as nearly balanced between normal and anomalous images. Category-scale evaluations use randomized subsets S1 (30), S2 (60), S3 (100), and the full 160 categories. MUAD models generally use 256×256 resolution for 100 epochs; Dinomaly follows its original configuration with a 392×392 crop from 448×448 input for 50,000 steps. ZSAD uses 0-shot evaluation; FSAD uses 1 or 4 normal target-class images as visual prompts, with results averaged over three random-seed runs. MVAD uses multiple views of each sample. Reports image- and pixel-level ROC, PR, maximum F1, and pixel-level PRO.

datasets.name: Real-IAD
datasets.eval_protocol: Used for 30-category comparisons with Real-IAD Variety in MUAD and ZSAD/FSAD tables, and as a pretraining dataset for the ADPretrain comparison. The paper does not specify the evaluation split or preprocessing for these runs.

datasets.name: MVTec AD
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as an independent few-shot test benchmark for ADPretrain models pretrained on Real-IAD or Real-IAD Variety; reports 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-shot results. The paper does not specify the test split or few-shot sampling protocol.

datasets.name: VisA
datasets.eval_protocol: Used as an independent few-shot test benchmark for ADPretrain models pretrained on Real-IAD or Real-IAD Variety; reports 1-, 2-, 4-, and 8-shot results. The paper does not specify the test split or few-shot sampling protocol.

evidence_standards.name: Three random-seed runs for FSAD
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports FSAD performance averaged over three runs with different random seeds, giving both mean and standard deviation. It does not specify a statistical test or a threshold for treating differences as real.

datasets.name: MVTec AD
datasets.eval_protocol: 15 categories; 3,629 training images and 1,725 test images. Training images are normal; test images have normal/abnormal labels and anomaly masks. Reports image-level AUROC for detection and pixel-level AUROC for segmentation. Single-model preprocessing: resize to 256×256, then center-crop to 224×224; ensemble preprocessing: resize to 366×366, then center-crop to 320×320; comparisons with PNI use resize to 512×512, then center-crop to 480×480. No data augmentation in the main evaluation.

datasets.name: BTAD
datasets.eval_protocol: Three product categories; 1,799 training images and 741 test images. Training images are normal; test images have normal/abnormal labels and anomaly masks. Reports image-level AUROC for detection and pixel-level AUROC for segmentation. ReConPatch uses a pretrained WideResNet-101 feature extractor with image size 480×480.

In the feature-dimension ablation, PatchCore and ReConPatch use WideResNet-50 and 1% coreset subsampling, with the same tested feature dimensions. The ensemble comparison uses 320×320 images and preprocessing as in PatchCore.

baselines.name: CFLOW-AD
baselines.fair_comparison: The reported MVTec results use WideResNet-50 at 256×256; the paper says these are the best results for each category at that image size.

baselines.name: PNI

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: One-class classification: train on one digit class as normal and treat the other nine classes as abnormal; about 6,000 training images per class, with a 10,000-image test set containing normal and abnormal classes. Images resized to 512 × 512 × 3. Global anomaly detection uses reconstruction loss.

datasets.name: CIFAR10
datasets.eval_protocol: One-class classification: train on one class as normal and treat the remaining classes as abnormal; train on 4,500 images per class and use the remaining 500 per class for performance verification. The test set has 10,000 normal and abnormal images. Images resized to 512 × 512 × 3. Global anomaly detection uses reconstruction loss.

datasets.name: MVTec Anomaly Detection (MVTecAD)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate all 15 categories; train only on defect-free images and test on defect-free and defective images. The dataset has 3,629 training/verification images and 1,725 test images, with original resolutions from 700 × 700 to 1024 × 1024. For PRO, increase the anomaly-score threshold until the average positive rate per pixel reaches 30%; localization is also evaluated with AUROC.

baselines.name: l2-CAE
baselines.fair_comparison: The paper says preprocessing and training were conducted under the same conditions for its ViT-versus-CNN encoder comparison; it does not specify further fairness details for the reported l2-CAE results.

controls.name: CNN encoder instead of ViT
controls.detail: The paper reports an experiment replacing the ViT encoder with a CNN while keeping data preprocessing and training conditions the same.
controls.rules_out: That any difference is due only to changed preprocessing or training conditions; the comparison tests the effect of the encoder choice.

datasets.name: MVTec-AD
datasets.eval_protocol: Few-shot evaluation with k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} nominal reference samples per category; test samples are scored at input resolutions 448 and 672. Three runs use the first, second, and third k training samples as references. Default preprocessing is agnostic: category-appropriate masking and reference rotations. Pixel-level maps use bilinear upsampling and Gaussian smoothing (σ=4.0).

datasets.name: VisA
datasets.eval_protocol: Few-shot evaluation with k ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} nominal reference samples per category; test samples are scored at input resolutions 448 and 672. Three runs use the first, second, and third k training samples as references. Default preprocessing is agnostic: category-appropriate masking and reference rotations. Pixel-level maps use bilinear upsampling and Gaussian smoothing (σ=4.0).

metrics.name: Pixel-level AUROC
metrics.caveat: Nominal pixels dominate the pixel counts (97.26% for MVTec-AD and 99.45% for VisA), so segmentation performance should not be assessed by AUROC alone; the paper also reports pixel-level F1-max and PRO.

controls.name: AnomalyDINO without preprocessing
controls.detail: The paper compares detection AUROC with and without its proposed preprocessing.
controls.rules_out: That the reported detection improvement over the unprocessed condition is absent when preprocessing is removed.

controls.name: Informed preprocessing
controls.detail: Compared with the default agnostic preprocessing; the informed setting uses knowledge of potential sample rotations.
controls.rules_out: That the reported preprocessing result depends on using the informed rather than the agnostic setting.

controls.name: Maximum of upsampled and smoothed patch distances
controls.detail: Compared with the default aggregation, the mean of the 1% highest patch distances.
controls.rules_out: That the result is explained merely by using an aggregation of patch distances; the comparison tests the proposed aggregation against the standard maximum.

evidence_standards.name: Three runs; report mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: Variation comes from the reference-sample choice: runs use the first k, second k, and third k training samples as references. The paper reports mean and standard deviation; it specifies no statistical test or threshold for declaring a difference real. It notes that GraphCore results have no reported standard deviations.

datasets.name: MVTec AD
datasets.eval_protocol: One-class evaluation: train on normal images and test on normal and anomalous images across 15 classes. For PaDiM and SPADE, resize to 256×256 and center-crop to 224×224; resize images and localization maps with bicubic interpolation and Gaussian-filter anomaly maps with σ=4. Localization uses patch-wise Mahalanobis scores; the image-level anomaly score is the maximum of the anomaly map.

datasets.name: Rd-MVTec AD
datasets.eval_protocol: Modified MVTec AD with random rotation from −10° to +10° and random crop from 256×256 to 224×224 applied to both train and test sets. Run preprocessing with 5 random seeds to create 5 dataset versions and average results. PaDiM and SPADE use the stated 256×256 resize and 224×224 center-crop preprocessing; anomaly maps are Gaussian-filtered with σ=4.

datasets.name: Shanghai Tech Campus (STC)
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluate on 274,515 training frames and 42,883 test frames across 13 scenes; training videos contain normal sequences and test videos contain anomalies. Resize images to 256×256 only; resize localization maps with bicubic interpolation and Gaussian-filter anomaly maps with σ=4. Report localization AUROC.

baselines.name: SPADE (WR50)
baselines.fair_comparison: PaDiM is also evaluated with a Wide ResNet-50-2 backbone, as used by SPADE, and the paper applies the same preprocessing to PaDiM and SPADE.

metrics.name: Localization AUROC
metrics.caveat: Biased in favor of large anomalies; the paper also reports PRO-score, which reflects localization performance across connected components.

controls.name: Single-layer and summed-layer PaDiM ablations
controls.detail: Compare PaDiM using individual ResNet18 layers and a Layers 1+2+3 version that sums the separate model outputs, against PaDiM modeling the three layers jointly.
controls.rules_out: That the gain comes merely from using or aggregating information from multiple semantic levels, rather than modeling correlations between them.

controls.name: PCA dimensionality reduction
controls.detail: Compare random feature selection with PCA at the same reduced embedding sizes of 100 and 200 dimensions.
controls.rules_out: That the reported performance of random dimensionality reduction is simply due to reducing the embedding dimension; the comparison tests the choice of reduction method.

confounds.name: The benefit comes from aggregating multiple layers, not modeling inter-layer correlations
confounds.detail: A multilevel representation could improve localization even without the paper’s claimed correlation modeling.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare the joint-Gaussian PaDiM model with the Layers 1+2+3 condition that sums separate layer-model outputs; PaDiM performs better on MVTec AD.

confounds.name: Random feature selection results depend on a lucky random selection
confounds.detail: A favorable randomly selected subset could account for the dimensionality-reduction results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Train 10 models with random feature selection and average their scores; report AUROC standard error of the mean between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁷.

evidence_standards.name: Random feature-selection runs
evidence_standards.detail: Train 10 models and average scores; report AUROC standard error of the mean between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻⁷.

evidence_standards.name: Rd-MVTec preprocessing runs
evidence_standards.detail: Create 5 dataset versions using random-seed preprocessing and average the results.

datasets.name: LOCO-Annotations
datasets.eval_protocol: 2,908 images total: 1,772 training and 1,136 testing images across juice bottle, breakfast box, pushpins, screw bag, and splicing connectors. The testing subset annotates logical anomalies only. Classification is evaluated against Normal/Abnormal ground-truth labels using accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score; comparisons use binary accuracy with variable-threshold optimization. The paper reports five experiment sets per category, averaged. Code-generation success is tested with 20 generations per category; reasoning is evaluated on five sets of successfully executed codes per category. Experiments use GPT-4. No image preprocessing is specified.

baselines.name: ST
baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

baselines.name: PEFM
baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

baselines.name: EfficientAD-S
baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

baselines.name: EfficientAD-M
baselines.fair_comparison: All competing methods were implemented in-house and compared on LOCO-Annotations; the comparison reports binary classification accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.caveat: The paper says traditional methods predominantly use AUROC, whereas LogiCode outputs discrete labels; it therefore reports binary accuracy with variable-threshold optimization.

metrics.name: Code generation success rate
metrics.caveat: The paper distinguishes correct executable code from missing code and errors; success requires execution without syntax errors and alignment with the logical anomaly rules.

metrics.name: Reasoning accuracy
metrics.caveat: Correct anomaly classification can still come with an inaccurate explanation; the paper evaluates explanations separately using human and LLM assessment.

confounds.name: Correct classification may not mean the anomaly explanation is correct
confounds.detail: The paper notes instances where LLMs classify anomalies correctly but provide inaccurate explanations, so classification performance alone would not establish reliable reasoning.
confounds.ruled_out_by: It separately evaluates reasoning accuracy against the ground-truth reasons, using human assessment by three researchers and GPT-4 automatic evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: Five experiment sets per category for binary classification
evidence_standards.detail: Results are averaged for accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score; the paper does not specify seeds, variance estimates, or statistical tests.

evidence_standards.name: Twenty code generations per category
evidence_standards.detail: Code-generation success rate is calculated from repeated generations and whether the code runs successfully and follows the logical rules.

evidence_standards.name: Five sets of successful codes per category for reasoning evaluation
evidence_standards.detail: Results are averaged; reasoning evaluation is restricted to codes that executed successfully.

evidence_standards.name: Three independent human evaluators
evidence_standards.detail: Researchers with relevant backgrounds independently assess explanations, and their assessments are averaged; GPT-4 is also used for automatic reasoning evaluation.

evidence_standards.name: GPT-4 evaluation setting
evidence_standards.detail: The paper states that all experiments are based on GPT-4; it does not specify decoding settings.

datasets.name: MVTec AD
datasets.eval_protocol: Train on normal samples; evaluate on 15 categories using 3,629 normal training samples and a test set of 467 normal and 1,258 anomalous samples. Report image-level and pixel-level AUROC. For texture categories, use only the local-branch estimation error. Resize images to 224×224 and normalize pixel intensities using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

datasets.name: MVTec LOCO AD
datasets.eval_protocol: Train on normal samples; evaluate on five object categories using 1,772 training, 304 validation, and 1,568 test samples. Report results separately for logical and structural anomalies using image-level AUROC and pixel-level sPRO. Resize images to 224×224 and normalize pixel intensities using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

datasets.name: Retinal-OCT
datasets.eval_protocol: Use disease-free samples as normal for training and evaluate image-level lesion detection on test samples containing normal cases and CNV, DME, and drusen abnormalities; the paper does not give split counts. Report image-level AUROC. Resize images to 224×224 and normalize pixel intensities using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

controls.name: Local branch alone
controls.detail: Evaluate the local-branch anomaly scores separately from the global branch and their fusion.
controls.rules_out: That the fused result depends only on the global branch; the branch comparison tests which anomaly types each branch detects.

controls.name: Global branch alone
controls.detail: Evaluate the global-branch anomaly scores separately from the local branch and their fusion.
controls.rules_out: That the fused result depends only on the local branch; the branch comparison tests whether the global branch helps with logical anomalies.

controls.name: Feature correspondence instead of feature estimation
controls.detail: Compare anomaly detection using feature correspondence with the proposed feature-estimation errors.
controls.rules_out: That the benefit of feature estimation is just the effect of using correspondence-based anomaly scores.

controls.name: Single-scale features
controls.detail: Compare detection using individual feature scales with the proposed multi-scale estimation-error fusion.
controls.rules_out: That the reported benefit comes from one feature scale rather than multi-scale fusion.

controls.name: Remove the entire semantic bottleneck
controls.detail: Use only the deepest encoder features for correspondence instead of the semantic bottleneck.
controls.rules_out: That the semantic bottleneck's performance benefit is present even without the bottleneck.

controls.name: Remove MS-PEM
controls.detail: Use only the deepest encoder features as input to SAM.
controls.rules_out: That multi-scale patch embedding contributes no benefit to the bottleneck.

controls.name: Remove SAM
controls.detail: Use the traditional ViT patch-embedding encoding-decoding process without additional semantic tokens; the model then performs feature correspondence.
controls.rules_out: That semantic aggregation by SAM contributes no benefit.

controls.name: Alternative SAM bottlenecks: PS and PGS
controls.detail: Compare the Patch-Spatial (PS) and Patch-Global-Spatial (PGS) structures with the proposed Patch-Spatial-Spatial (PSS) structure.
controls.rules_out: That the reported performance is independent of the SAM structure.

confounds.name: Feature-correspondence scores may produce false positives rather than reflect anomaly evidence
confounds.detail: Global features generated from the semantic bottleneck only roughly approximate local features, so a correspondence discrepancy could be noise rather than a meaningful anomaly signal.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare feature-estimation scoring against feature-correspondence scoring; the paper reports better detection with estimation and illustrates correspondence-related false-positive noise.

confounds.name: The apparent logical-anomaly benefit could come from the local branch, rather than global semantic detection
confounds.detail: A fused score could perform well without the global branch actually contributing to logical-anomaly detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare local- and global-branch results separately on MVTec LOCO AD; the paper reports the global branch is more effective for logical anomalies and the local branch for structural anomalies.

datasets.name: MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Use one class as normal and samples from the other classes as anomalies; vary contamination ratio ρ from 0.00 to 0.20. Test labels are 0 for the normal class and 1 for the other classes. Evaluate using ROC curves and AUC. Repeat training-set generation 10 times for each of the nine anomaly classes, yielding 90 experiments per contamination ratio; report average results.

datasets.name: Fashion-MNIST
datasets.eval_protocol: Use one class as normal and samples from the other classes as anomalies; vary contamination ratio ρ from 0.00 to 0.20. Test labels are 0 for the normal class and 1 for the other classes. Evaluate using ROC curves and AUC. Repeat training-set generation 10 times for each of the nine anomaly classes, yielding 90 experiments per contamination ratio; report average results.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the paper's shared dataset, class, and contamination-ratio evaluation setups; no further matching is stated.

evidence_standards.detail: The tables report values with ± terms, but the paper does not specify what those terms represent or describe a statistical test or threshold for deciding that a difference is real.

datasets.name: UCSD Ped2
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the normal-only training split (16 videos) and test split (12 videos, including anomalous events). Evaluates frame-level AUROC by varying the anomaly-score threshold, reporting micro-averaged AUROC over all frames and macro-averaged AUROC averaged across videos. Uses object-detection confidence threshold 0.5; because of the low resolution, uses B=1 velocity orientation bin and relies on velocity and deep features, without pose features.

datasets.name: CUHK Avenue
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the normal-only training split (16 videos) and test split (21 videos, including anomalous events). Evaluates frame-level AUROC by varying the anomaly-score threshold, reporting micro-averaged AUROC over all frames and macro-averaged AUROC averaged across videos. Uses object-detection confidence threshold 0.8 and B=8 velocity orientation bins.

datasets.name: ShanghaiTech Campus
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the normal-only training split (330 videos) and test split (107 videos, including anomalous events). Evaluates frame-level AUROC by varying the anomaly-score threshold, reporting micro-averaged AUROC over all frames and macro-averaged AUROC averaged across videos. Uses object-detection confidence threshold 0.8 and B=8 velocity orientation bins.

controls.name: Pose features only
controls.detail: Scores using pose features without deep or velocity features; evaluated where pose extraction is feasible.
controls.rules_out: Shows the performance of the pose component without the other feature components.

controls.name: Deep features only
controls.detail: Scores using deep features without pose or velocity features.
controls.rules_out: Shows the performance of the deep-feature component without the other feature components.

controls.name: Velocity features only
controls.detail: Scores using velocity features without pose or deep features.
controls.rules_out: Shows the performance of the velocity component without the other feature components.

controls.name: Pose and deep features, without velocity
controls.detail: Combines pose and deep features while omitting velocity features; evaluated where pose extraction is feasible.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the combination can perform without the velocity component.

controls.name: Deep and velocity features, without pose
controls.detail: Combines deep and velocity features without pose features; used on Ped2, where pose extraction is not feasible, and also evaluated on the other datasets.
controls.rules_out: Tests the combination without the pose component.

controls.name: Pose and velocity features, without deep features
controls.detail: Combines pose and velocity features while omitting deep features; evaluated where pose extraction is feasible.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the combination can perform without the deep-feature component.

confounds.name: Performance depends on a particular optical-flow or object-detection backbone rather than the feature design
confounds.detail: The headline performance could be specific to the selected FlowNet2 flow extractor or Mask R-CNN detector.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compared velocity-feature AUROC using FlowNet2 versus RAFT on Avenue and ShanghaiTech, and Mask R-CNN versus YOLO-v8 on those datasets; the authors conclude effectiveness is primarily driven by feature design rather than a specific backbone.

confounds.name: Deep-feature performance depends on the particular image encoder CLIP
confounds.detail: The contribution of deep features could be specific to the selected pretrained CLIP image encoder.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compared object-level DINO features with CLIP on Avenue and ShanghaiTech; DINO performed slightly worse than CLIP but better than the tested video encoders.

datasets.name: Arrhythmia

metrics.name: F1-score
metrics.caveat: The paper shows it is sensitive to test-set contamination and threshold selection, and therefore can give misleading comparisons across evaluation protocols or datasets. It recommends AUC instead.

metrics.name: AVPR
metrics.caveat: The paper shows it is sensitive to test-set contamination and can give misleading comparisons across evaluation protocols or datasets. It recommends AUC instead.

confounds.name: F1-score and AVPR gains arise only from using a test-derived threshold
confounds.detail: The increase in these metrics as test contamination rises might be attributed solely to recalibrating the threshold on the test set.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper also analyzes a constant-threshold setting and shows that F1-score and AVPR increase with test contamination there as well; the test-derived-threshold setting is shown to increase the bias further.

confounds.name: Metric gains arise because the anomaly detector changes as the test set changes
confounds.detail: An apparent gain could reflect changes in model training or detector capability rather than the test-set contamination rate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: In the contamination-sensitivity experiment, the clean training set is fixed while the number of anomalies added to the test set varies; the paper observes F1-score and AVPR increasing.

evidence_standards.name: 100 runs; mean and standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The paper states that all experiments are run 100 times and reports means with standard deviations. It specifies no statistical test, confidence interval, or margin for treating results as equivalent.

controls.name: Unmodified CLIP
controls.detail: The paper reports vanilla CLIP alongside AnoCLIP for zero-shot anomaly detection and localization.

controls.name: QKV attention
controls.detail: Uses the original CLIP QKV attention for patch tokens instead of the proposed local-aware extraction.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the localization result depends on changing the attention mechanism.

controls.name: V tokens from the last layer
controls.detail: Uses values from the final transformer layer as patch tokens, without multi-layer V-V attention.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether multi-layer V-V attention improves over using last-layer values alone.

controls.name: V-V attention in the last layer only
controls.detail: Uses V-V attention only in the final layer rather than accumulating it across multiple layers.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the multi-layer use of V-V attention contributes beyond a final-layer change.

controls.name: Base prompts
controls.detail: Uses base prompts without contrastive-state or domain-aware prompt additions.
controls.rules_out: Provides a prompt baseline for the effects of the proposed prompt additions.

controls.name: +CS Prompt
controls.detail: Adds contrastive-state prompts to the base prompts, without the domain-aware prompt addition.
controls.rules_out: Separates the reported contribution of contrastive-state prompting from the further addition of domain-aware prompts.

controls.name: Linear Probe adapter optimization
controls.detail: Optimizes the adapter using a linear probe rather than the proposed text-token initialization and dual-task optimization.
controls.rules_out: Tests whether the proposed adapter optimization performs better than the linear-probe alternative.

controls.name: AnoCLIP without TTA
controls.detail: Reports AnoCLIP alongside AnoCLIP+, which applies test-time adaptation.
controls.rules_out: Provides a reference for the effect of applying TTA to AnoCLIP.

evidence_standards.name: Five random seeds; mean and variance
evidence_standards.detail: The paper reports AnoCLIP+ results as mean and variance over 5 random seeds. TTA uses 5 optimization epochs in the reported experiments; no statistical test or threshold for treating differences as real is stated.

baselines.fair_comparison: The paper reports AnomalyCLIP results supplied at resolution 240, but notes that it uses ViT-L/14-336 while SDP/SDP+ use ViT-B/16+.

baselines.name: CLIP Surgery
baselines.fair_comparison: The comparison configuration uses the ViT-B/16+ CLIP backbone at 240 resolution; CLIP Surgery adds architecture-surgery layers only to the last six layers and uses only the final-layer output.

metrics.name: AUROC
metrics.caveat: The paper notes that pixel-level AUROC can let one correctly segmented large region compensate for many inaccurately segmented small regions; it reports F1-max, AP, and PRO alongside it for segmentation.

metrics.name: F1-max
metrics.caveat: It is the F1 score at the optimal threshold; the paper reports AUROC and AP alongside it, and PRO as an additional segmentation metric.

metrics.name: PRO
metrics.caveat: It treats anomaly regions of any size equally; the paper reports it alongside pixel-level AUROC, F1-max, and AP for segmentation.

controls.name: Direct cosine similarity on unaligned image feature maps
controls.detail: Compute anomaly maps directly from the original patch/image feature maps and text features, without SDP surgery or the SDP+ learned mapping.
controls.rules_out: That the reported segmentation behavior is simply what direct CLIP image-text similarity produces; the paper compares its very poor segmentation results with SDP/SDP+.

controls.name: Mean-vector text representation
controls.detail: Use the mean of sampled normal and abnormal text features instead of the selected DBSCAN representative vectors in the RVS comparison on MVTec-AD.
controls.rules_out: That the RVS result is merely due to averaging text prompts; the comparison tests whether the DBSCAN representative-vector choice changes performance.

controls.name: Individual block outputs and partial block combinations
controls.detail: Compare SDP and SDP+ using each block separately, the last two blocks, the last three blocks, and all blocks on MVTec-AD.
controls.rules_out: That the staged model's result is explained by a single favorable block; the all-block condition is compared with single-block and partial combinations.

controls.name: SDP without SDP+'s fine-tuned linear layers
controls.detail: Compare the no-fine-tuning SDP condition with SDP+, which adds and trains linear layers while freezing CLIP.
controls.rules_out: That SDP+'s gains are present without the learned feature mapping; the comparison measures the added mapping condition against the model without it.

confounds.name: SDP+ overfits the cross-training dataset
confounds.detail: The authors acknowledge that training across datasets may introduce overfitting, which could account for performance differences without generalizable feature alignment.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out by a reported validation measurement; the authors say an extra validation set could mitigate the issue.

confounds.name: More complex mapping networks fit the training data rather than learning a general adjustment
confounds.detail: The paper says that multiple linear layers or activations may overfit, so training loss convergence could fail to translate into test performance.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compare test-set results for 3-layer and 5-layer mappings, with and without ReLU, at the original and 10-times-lower learning rates, against the single-linear-layer model; the authors note that training-loss convergence alone does not ensure better test performance.

confounds.name: Text-prompt sampling or outliers, rather than the representative-vector strategy, determine the result
confounds.detail: The authors describe prompt performance as sensitive and potentially random, with inappropriate sampled prompts acting as outliers.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On MVTec-AD, compare mean, PCA, KDE, Mean Shift, and DBSCAN representative-vector methods; the paper reports that DBSCAN improves several metrics over the mean.

confounds.name: Metric choice makes apparent gains misleading
confounds.detail: The authors state that pixel-level AUROC can be high when one large region is segmented correctly despite many small-region errors, and that metrics have different biases.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Report multiple metrics alongside AUROC, including F1-max, AP, and PRO; PRO treats anomaly regions of any size equally.

evidence_standards.name: Model selection by image-level AUROC
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says it reports the model with the highest image-level AUROC.

evidence_standards.name: Reported default training and model configuration
evidence_standards.detail: Unless otherwise stated, use CLIP ViT-B/16+ pretrained on LAION-400M at image resolution 240; SDP+ trains added linear layers for 5 epochs with batch size 8, Adam, and fixed learning rate 1e-4. The paper does not state seed counts, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

metrics.name: QQ-plot calibration of the contamination-factor posterior
Mean absolute error (MAE) of the contamination-factor point estimate
F1 deterioration
metrics.caveat: Ranking errors by the anomaly detector can affect F1 even with the correct contamination factor; the paper evaluates only the detector(s) achieving the greatest F1 at the true contamination factor for each dataset. It also notes that an estimated, incorrect contamination factor can sometimes yield higher F1 than the true value because detector rankings are imperfect; false alarms and false negatives are additionally reported in the supplement.

confounds.name: F1 differences may reflect anomaly-detector ranking quality rather than contamination-factor estimation
confounds.detail: Detectors that rank samples poorly can have poor F1 even when thresholded using the correct contamination factor, so the headline F1 comparison could reflect detector quality rather than the estimate.
confounds.ruled_out_by: For each dataset, compare F1 only for the detector(s) achieving the greatest F1 when thresholded using the true contamination factor.

confounds.name: Results may depend on the chosen p0 and p_high hyperparameters
confounds.detail: The estimated posterior and its calibration could be an artifact of the default hyperparameter choices rather than a robust property of the method.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Vary p0 and p_high one at a time over 0.0001, 0.001, 0.05, and 0.1; inspect QQ calibration plots and compare MAE across variants.

confounds.name: Posterior calibration may depend on the number or selection of anomaly detectors
confounds.detail: The reported calibration could depend on using all 10 detectors rather than being robust to detector-set size or selection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Repeat experiments 10 times with randomly selected detector subsets at M=3, 5, and 7, and compare calibration curves and variation.

evidence_standards.name: Variational-inference repeat runs
evidence_standards.detail: Run variational inference 10 times and concatenate samples to reduce the risk of biased distributions from local minima.

evidence_standards.name: Reported variation across experiments
evidence_standards.detail: Report MAE and F1 deterioration as mean ± standard deviation; report average method ranks with standard deviation.

evidence_standards.name: Repeated detector-subset experiments
evidence_standards.detail: For M=3, 5, and 7, run experiments 10 times using different randomly chosen detectors and show uncertainty across these repeats.

evidence_standards.name: Calibration deviation criterion reported
evidence_standards.detail: Assess calibration by QQ-plot empirical frequencies against expected probabilities; report deviations under 5% in more than 76% of cases and no deviations over 10%.

metrics.name: Point-adjust F1
metrics.caveat: A single detected point in an anomalous segment makes every point in that segment count as detected, so sparse or random predictions can obtain very high scores. The paper contrasts it with point-wise, composite, and event-wise evaluation.

metrics.name: Point-wise F1
metrics.caveat: It can vary with dataset contamination rate and can be dominated by long anomalous events; it also does not show the false-alarm burden or how many events were detected. The paper reports FAR and event-aware metrics, including detected-event counts, alongside it.

metrics.name: Composite F1 (F1_C)
metrics.caveat: Uses event-level recall but point-level precision, so its precision remains tied to point-level counts. The paper reports event-wise F1 and detected-event and false-alarm-segment counts alongside it.

metrics.name: Event-wise F1 (F1_E)
metrics.caveat: An event-wise precision based only on detected and false-alarm segments would give a perfect score to an algorithm that alarms at every point; the paper includes point-level FAR in event-wise precision to prevent this.

metrics.name: Detected events (TP_E) and non-overlapping predicted segments (FP_E)
metrics.caveat: The paper reports these counts alongside the F1 metrics to show how many ground-truth events were detected and how many predicted anomalous segments did not overlap any event.

controls.name: Untrained Anomaly Transformer and NCAD
controls.detail: The paper evaluated untrained versions and reports that they achieved essentially the same high point-adjust scores as the trained versions.
controls.rules_out: That the high point-adjust scores necessarily demonstrate that the trained models learned useful anomaly-detection behavior.

controls.name: Randomly selected anomalous points
controls.detail: The paper evaluates predictions that randomly tag a fixed number of points as anomalous; with 1000 selected points, it reports average point-adjust F1 of about 0.95 on SWaT and Wadi and 0.98 on PSM.
controls.rules_out: That high point-adjust scores necessarily require a detector that identifies anomalies meaningfully.

confounds.name: High point-adjust scores arise from arbitrary or untrained predictions rather than learned detection
confounds.detail: The headline point-adjust score could be high even if a model's outputs do not encode useful anomaly detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates untrained Anomaly Transformer and NCAD versions and finds essentially the same high point-adjust scores; it also evaluates randomly selected anomalous points and obtains high scores.

confounds.name: High point-wise F1 on PSM reflects its high anomaly prevalence and predictions of most points as anomalous
confounds.detail: A seemingly strong point-wise F1 could result from the dataset's 27.76% contamination rate rather than selective detection.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper examines the algorithms' outputs, notes that Anomaly Transformer and NCAD predict all or most points as anomalous, and reports event-wise F1, which incorporates FAR, alongside point-wise F1.

datasets.name: MVTec LOCO AD

The method uses k=2 nearest normal references; images are resized to 224×224 and normalized using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

datasets.name: MVTec AD

Evaluation reports image- and pixel-level AUROC for structural anomalies; pixel annotations are provided. The method uses k=2 nearest normal references; images are resized to 224×224 and normalized using ImageNet mean and standard deviation. SAM is filtered to segment the single object.

datasets.name: DigitAnatomy

The paper does not specify the split or sample counts. It uses the lightweight SAM-LAD variant that scores only unmatched objects. Images are resized to 224×224 and normalized using ImageNet mean and standard deviation.

metrics.name: Image-level AUROC

metrics.name: sPRO
metrics.caveat: It saturates once overlap with ground truth reaches the dataset-provided saturation threshold; reported with per-pixel false-positive rate of 5%.

controls.name: GAP and GMP feature-compression replacements for DCGA
controls.detail: The paper compares global average pooling and global max pooling with its DCGA module on MVTec LOCO AD, reporting matching precision, recall, F1, detection AUROC, and segmentation sPRO.
controls.rules_out: That the reported DCGA gains are explained merely by compressing object features into vectors; the comparisons test the proposed compression mechanism against pooling alternatives.

controls.name: No-upsampling (1×) feature maps
controls.detail: The FeatUp ablation compares the original 1× feature maps with the main 8× setting and other upsampling factors on MVTec LOCO AD.
controls.rules_out: That the reported performance requires no spatial upsampling; the 1× condition provides the no-FeatUp comparison.

controls.name: Wide-ResNet50 and Swin-Transformer backbones
controls.detail: The backbone ablation compares these alternatives with DINOv2 on MVTec LOCO AD, using detection AUROC and segmentation sPRO.
controls.rules_out: That the reported result is independent of the selected feature extractor; the comparison tests the DINOv2 choice against the named alternatives.

confounds.name: Object matching accuracy may account for the detection results
confounds.detail: The paper identifies OMM as central to logical anomaly detection, while similar objects in categories such as pushpins and splicing connectors make matching less accurate; this could affect the headline performance attributed to the full framework.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper reports OMM matching precision, recall, and F1 by category and mean on MVTec LOCO AD and DigitAnatomy, and notes that AMM reduces dependence on matching accuracy. This measures the concern but does not eliminate it.

confounds.name: Similar same-category objects and SAM segmentation granularity can cause missed logical anomalies
confounds.detail: The authors concede that SAM-LAD can fail when multiple similar objects of the same category occur in a scene, because SAM segmentation may be too fine or too coarse and OMM may fail to identify extra objects.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Not ruled out; the paper presents a pushpins failure case in Figure 14 and identifies this as a limitation.

metrics.name: Precision@k
metrics.caveat: Uses only the k highest anomaly scores, so the choice of k matters; the paper reports threshold-independent AUC-, Range-AUC-, and VUS-based measures alongside it.

metrics.name: Precision
metrics.caveat: Requires thresholding and is sensitive to threshold choice; threshold-based measures are also affected by noise and the normal/abnormal ratio. The paper reports threshold-independent measures alongside them.

metrics.name: Recall
metrics.caveat: Requires thresholding and is sensitive to threshold choice; point-based scoring does not adequately handle range anomalies and misalignment. The paper reports threshold-independent and range-based measures alongside it.

metrics.name: F-score
metrics.caveat: Requires thresholding, can vary substantially with the threshold, and point-based scoring does not adequately handle range anomalies or misalignment. The paper reports AUC-, Range-AUC-, and VUS-based measures alongside it.

metrics.name: Rprecision
metrics.caveat: Still requires a threshold and range-based measures have tunable parameters; the paper reports threshold-independent Range-AUC and VUS measures alongside it.

metrics.name: Rrecall
metrics.caveat: Still requires a threshold and range-based measures have tunable parameters; the paper reports threshold-independent Range-AUC and VUS measures alongside it.

metrics.name: RF-score
metrics.caveat: Still requires a threshold and range-based measures have tunable parameters; the paper reports threshold-independent Range-AUC and VUS measures alongside it.

metrics.name: AUC-ROC
metrics.caveat: Threshold-independent, but designed for point-based anomalies and does not adequately account for range anomalies or label/score misalignment. The paper reports Range-AUC-ROC and VUS-ROC alongside it.

metrics.name: AUC-PR
metrics.caveat: Threshold-independent, but designed for point-based anomalies and can be sensitive to lag; the paper also notes PR measures vary with the normal/abnormal ratio. The paper reports Range-AUC-PR and VUS-PR alongside it.

metrics.name: R-AUC-ROC
metrics.caveat: Its result can depend strongly on the chosen buffer length; VUS-ROC evaluates across buffer lengths.

metrics.name: R-AUC-PR
metrics.caveat: Its result can depend strongly on the chosen buffer length, and PR-based measures vary with the normal/abnormal ratio; VUS-PR evaluates across buffer lengths.

metrics.name: VUS-ROC
metrics.caveat: More expensive to compute than AUC-based measures; the paper reports optimized implementations that retain the naive implementation's exact values.

metrics.name: VUS-PR
metrics.caveat: More expensive to compute than AUC-based measures and, as a precision-based measure, varies with the normal/abnormal ratio; the paper reports optimized implementations that retain the naive implementation's exact values.

metrics.name: Standard deviation of scores under perturbation
metrics.caveat: Used as a robustness measure: smaller standard deviation indicates greater robustness to the varied lag, noise, or normal/abnormal ratio.

metrics.name: Z-test
metrics.caveat: Used to assess separation between scores for manually selected accurate and inaccurate methods; the paper reports average Z-tests across method pairs and datasets.

metrics.name: Shannon entropy of method ranks
metrics.caveat: Used as a consistency measure across series within a dataset; lower rank entropy is interpreted as more consistent rankings.

metrics.name: Execution time
metrics.caveat: VUS computation is slower than AUC-based approaches; the paper reports optimized VUS implementations and compares their execution time with the naive implementation.

controls.name: Naive VUS implementation
controls.detail: The unoptimized implementation is compared with VUSopt and VUSopt^mem, which use static/dynamic sections and, for the memory variant, stored predictions.
controls.rules_out: The optimized implementations' speedup being due to changing the computed measure: the paper states the optimized versions return the same values as naive VUS.

confounds.name: Range-AUC results reflect the chosen buffer length or period estimate rather than method quality
confounds.detail: The paper notes that different period estimates and multi-period time series can produce different buffer lengths, and that a poorly set buffer length can strongly influence Range-AUC.
confounds.ruled_out_by: Compute VUS across buffer lengths from zero to the selected maximum, making the measure independent of a single buffer-length choice; evaluate robustness across lag and other perturbations.

evidence_standards.name: Robustness perturbations: 10 values per factor
evidence_standards.detail: For each anomaly score, vary lag over [-0.25ℓ, 0.25ℓ], noise over [-0.05(max(S_T)-min(S_T)), 0.05(max(S_T)-min(S_T))], or normal/abnormal ratio over [0.01, 0.2]; compute the standard deviation across the ten values.

evidence_standards.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank test, α = 0.1
evidence_standards.detail: Used for critical-difference comparisons of robustness across time series.

evidence_standards.name: Friedman test followed by post-hoc Wilcoxon test, α = 0.1
evidence_standards.detail: Used for critical-difference comparisons of measure rankings.

evidence_standards.name: Separability Z-test
evidence_standards.detail: Inject lag and noise into each selected accurate/inaccurate method pair 50 times, then use a Z-test to compare the resulting score distributions; aggregate average Z-tests across pairs and datasets.

evidence_standards.name: Ten anomaly-score runs for consistency analysis
evidence_standards.detail: The paper computes anomaly scores ten times and uses average accuracy for its rank-consistency analysis.

evidence_standards.name: Ten execution-time runs
evidence_standards.detail: Synthetic-series execution times are averaged over ten runs; the figures show standard-deviation envelopes.

controls.rules_out: That the results are unaffected by the region-extraction choice or require only the proposed Adaptive scaled OTSU.

controls.name: Feature ablations
controls.detail: The paper compares area alone (A), area plus color (A+Co), area plus connectivity (A+H), and area plus color and connectivity (A+Co+H).
controls.rules_out: That the results require all selected features, and measures the contribution of color and connectivity alongside area.

controls.name: Supervised-feature clustering in place of DINO features
controls.detail: The paper fixes the other settings and replaces the DINO backbone with ImageNet-supervised WideResNet-50 layer-2 features for segmentation; it also tries layer 3 and layer 4.
controls.rules_out: That the segmentation result is independent of the selected pretrained feature representation.

confounds.name: Deep pretrained features may implicitly capture the metrological information attributed to explicit area and counting features
confounds.detail: If deep features already reliably represented component quantities, the logical-anomaly results would not establish the need for ComAD’s explicit metrological features.
confounds.ruled_out_by: On the constructed circle-count dataset, the paper tests global average pooling and masked-sum features from WideResNet-50 layer 2 and DINO’s first block, and visualizes category distributions with t-SNE. It reports that the features become ineffective as circle counts increase, with masked sum and supervised features performing relatively better but not substantially changing the result.

evidence_standards.name: Five runs; report the average
evidence_standards.detail: The paper says all experiments are run five times and the average is used as the result. It does not state a variance measure, confidence interval, statistical test, or margin for treating results as ties.

datasets.name: Valeo Anomaly Dataset (VAD)
datasets.eval_protocol: Uses the predefined train/test split: 2,000 good and 1,000 bad training images; 1,000 good and 1,000 bad test images, including 165 bad images with defect types absent from training. Evaluates one-class (no real bad images for training; SegAD uses artificial defects), high-shot supervised (1,000 bad training images), and low-shot supervised (100 randomly selected bad training images). The same 2,000 good training images are split between base-model and SegAD training; low-shot selection and training/splits use 5 seeds. Images are resized to 256×256 and training augmentations are removed, except for artificial defects used to train SegAD in the one-class benchmark. Reports classification AUROC and FPR@95TPR.

datasets.name: VisA
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluates the 12-class supervised benchmark by moving 10 randomly selected bad images per class from test to train and reporting results over 10 seeds. The base anomaly detectors use good training images; for RD4AD, 90% of training images train the detector and 10% train SegAD, while EfficientAD’s 10% validation set is also used to train SegAD. Segmentation maps are created with SAM, with static component maps added for pcb1–4. Images are resized to 256×256 and training augmentations are removed. Reports classification AUROC and FPR@95TPR; no variance is shown in the results table.

baselines.name: PatchCore
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared both alone and as an input to SegAD. The paper resizes images to 256×256 and removes training augmentations for the model comparisons; VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs. It does not specify further equality of training data across all methods.

baselines.name: FastFlow
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared both alone and as an input to SegAD. The paper resizes images to 256×256 and removes training augmentations for the model comparisons; VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs. It does not specify further equality of training data across all methods.

baselines.name: RD4AD (Reverse Distillation)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared both alone and as an input to SegAD. The paper resizes images to 256×256 and removes training augmentations for the model comparisons; VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs. For VisA, 90% of good training images train RD4AD and 10% train SegAD.

baselines.name: EfficientAD
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared both alone and as an input to SegAD. The paper resizes images to 256×256 and removes training augmentations for the model comparisons; VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs. For VisA, the 10% validation set used to normalize anomaly maps is also used to train SegAD.

baselines.name: DevNet
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the paper’s shared 256×256 image resolution and without training augmentations; VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs. The paper does not specify further equality of training data across all methods.

baselines.name: DRA
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the paper’s shared 256×256 image resolution and without training augmentations; VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs. The paper notes DRA’s original 448×448 resolution gives 92.8 classification AUROC on VAD, but uses 256×256 for the comparison.

baselines.name: WRN (Wide ResNet50)
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared under the paper’s shared 256×256 image resolution and without training augmentations. Its classifier is trained separately on 80% of the full VAD training set (1,600 good and 800 bad images); VAD results are averaged over 5 seeds/training runs.

baselines.name: BT (Boosted Tree)
baselines.fair_comparison: In the VAD high-shot ablation, compared with BRF using the same segmentation map and features.

baselines.name: RF (Random Forest)
baselines.fair_comparison: In the VAD high-shot ablation, compared with BRF using the same segmentation map and features.

metrics.name: Classification AUROC (Cl. AUROC)
metrics.caveat: A strong supervised-classifier result can fail to reflect detection of unseen defect types: the paper shows WRN’s unseen-defect score distribution shifted low. It also reports FPR@95TPR and visualizes score distributions, but gives no separate unseen-only metric.

metrics.name: FPR@95TPR
metrics.caveat: The paper defines this as the percentage of good parts falsely classified as defective when 95% of bad parts are correctly classified; it reports this alongside classification AUROC.

controls.name: Standalone one-class anomaly detector
controls.detail: Runs the underlying detector alone as well as the corresponding detector-plus-SegAD setup; the standalone detector uses the maximum anomaly-map value as its score.
controls.rules_out: That gains from adding SegAD are merely due to using a different underlying anomaly detector.

controls.name: One Seg ablation
controls.detail: Uses SegAD’s feature vector and BRF but omits the segmentation map.
controls.rules_out: That the segmentation map is unnecessary for the reported improvement.

controls.name: Max ablation
controls.detail: Uses segmentation and BRF, but uses the maximum anomaly-map value per segment rather than SegAD’s proposed statistics.
controls.rules_out: That the proposed anomaly-map statistics are unnecessary for the reported improvement.

controls.name: BT ablation
controls.detail: Uses SegAD’s features and segmentation map with a Boosted Tree instead of BRF.
controls.rules_out: That the result is simply due to the features and segmentation map, rather than the BRF choice.

controls.name: RF ablation
controls.detail: Uses SegAD’s features and segmentation map with a Random Forest instead of BRF.
controls.rules_out: That the result is simply due to the features and segmentation map, rather than the BRF choice.

confounds.name: Improvement reflects detection of seen defects but not generalization to unseen defects
confounds.detail: A supervised method could score well by learning the defect types available in training while missing the rare, unseen VAD defect types.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper includes 165 test images with unseen defect types and visualizes score distributions for good, bad, and unseen-bad parts; it reports that SegAD’s unseen-defect scores have a distribution similar to seen defects, unlike WRN’s shifted-low unseen-defect scores.

confounds.name: Differences in input resolution explain method comparisons
confounds.detail: DRA’s original 448×448 resolution gives better VAD results than running it at 256×256, so comparisons at different resolutions could favor a method for reasons unrelated to the method itself.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper resizes images to 256×256 for comparisons and reports the 448×448 DRA result separately.

confounds.name: Differences in training augmentations explain method comparisons
confounds.detail: Augmentations may suit particular tasks or methods and could affect their relative results.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper removes existing augmentations from the compared methods and uses no training augmentations in the experiments, except the artificial-defect generation required for SegAD’s one-class training setup.

evidence_standards.name: VAD results over 5 seeds and training runs, reported as mean ± standard deviation
evidence_standards.detail: The seeds are used for training and for the SegAD training-set split; the paper states that results are averaged over the 5 runs.

evidence_standards.name: VisA results over 10 seeds
evidence_standards.detail: The 10 randomly selected bad training images are selected across 10 seeds; the results table does not report standard deviations or a statistical test.

datasets.name: Machine-Temp
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated against ground truth using classical sample-based precision/recall, RP/RR, TaP/TaR, and affiliation metrics, with Greenhouse, LSTM-AD, and Luminol TSB predictions. 17,682 samples, 6% anomalous, 2 anomalous events; no split or trial count reported.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated against ground truth using classical sample-based precision/recall, RP/RR, TaP/TaR, and affiliation metrics, with Greenhouse, LSTM-AD, and Luminol TSB predictions. 2,307 samples, 27% anomalous, 3 anomalous events; no split or trial count reported.

datasets.name: Twitter-AAPL
datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated against ground truth using classical sample-based precision/recall, RP/RR, TaP/TaR, and affiliation metrics, with Greenhouse, LSTM-AD, and Luminol TSB predictions. 11,889 samples, 7% anomalous, 2 anomalous events; no split or trial count reported.

datasets.eval_protocol: Evaluated against ground truth using classical sample-based precision/recall, RP/RR, TaP/TaR, and affiliation metrics, with iForest, OCSVM, and seq2seq predictions. 449,919 samples, 12% anomalous, 35 anomalous events; no split or trial count reported.

baselines.fair_comparison: Applied to the same dataset prediction outputs used for the other metric comparisons.

baselines.fair_comparison: Applied to the same dataset prediction outputs used for the other metric comparisons; the paper uses the default parameters for the stated theoretical adversary result.

baselines.name: TaP/TaR (time-aware precision/recall)
baselines.fair_comparison: Applied to the same dataset prediction outputs used for the other metric comparisons; the paper uses the default parameters for the stated theoretical adversary result.

baselines.name: Greenhouse
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same datasets and with the same evaluation metrics as the other prediction algorithms; no matched training or tuning protocol is reported.

baselines.name: LSTM-AD
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same datasets and with the same evaluation metrics as the other prediction algorithms; no matched training or tuning protocol is reported.

baselines.name: Luminol TSB
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on the same datasets and with the same evaluation metrics as the other prediction algorithms; no matched training or tuning protocol is reported.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on SWaT with the same evaluation metrics as the other prediction algorithms; no matched training or tuning protocol is reported.

baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on SWaT with the same evaluation metrics as the other prediction algorithms; no matched training or tuning protocol is reported.

baselines.name: seq2seq
baselines.fair_comparison: Compared on SWaT with the same evaluation metrics as the other prediction algorithms; no matched training or tuning protocol is reported.

baselines.name: trivial prediction
baselines.fair_comparison: Included alongside the other predictions in the metric comparison on the same datasets; the paper does not report a matched tuning protocol.

baselines.name: adversary algorithm
baselines.fair_comparison: Included alongside the other predictions in the metric comparison on the same datasets; the paper defines it from a trivial event by alternating positive and negative samples within it and labeling all samples outside it positive.

metrics.name: Classical sample-based precision and recall
metrics.caveat: They do not account for temporal adjacency or event duration; the paper compares them with range-based metrics and affiliation precision/recall.

metrics.name: RP/RR (range precision/recall)
metrics.caveat: The adversary predictions achieve high scores despite providing no informative anomaly localization; the paper reports affiliation and classical metrics alongside them.

metrics.name: TaP/TaR (time-aware precision/recall)
metrics.caveat: The adversary predictions achieve high scores despite providing no informative anomaly localization; the paper reports affiliation and classical metrics alongside them.

metrics.name: Affiliation precision and recall
metrics.caveat: Scores around 0.5 correspond to performance as bad as a random prediction under the metric's construction; the paper interprets scores against that random-sampling reference and also reports per-event results.

metrics.name: F1-score
metrics.caveat: The paper says further research is needed to obtain theoretical bounds on the variance of summarized metrics; it reports precision and recall alongside F1.

confounds.name: High range-metric scores can result from adversarial prediction construction rather than informative anomaly localization
confounds.detail: The adversary labels nearly all samples positive while arranging many predictions around a trivial event, so its high range-metric scores could appear to indicate a strong detector even though the predictions do not meaningfully locate anomalies.
confounds.ruled_out_by: The paper evaluates the adversary predictions on the selected datasets and reports their scores under classical precision/recall, RP/RR, TaP/TaR, and affiliation metrics; the affiliation precision is about 0.50 for the adversary results, interpreted as no better than random.
